title: 2023 operating budget review and strategic investments
subtitle: Traffic calming, trails, recreation access, fleet greening, new staff positions, golf, parking and gas utility questions
overview: The Finance and Corporate Services Committee held a special meeting to review the proposed 2023 operating budget. Staff presented a 4.8% property tax increase, about $56 a year for the average home, and a 4.5% water utility increase of about $42. Together that is about $98 a year. The committee also heard from Kitchener Public Library and Centre in the Square about their budgets.

Most of the day went to $1.5M in unallocated money from LED streetlight savings, which could fund strategic investments in housing, fleet greening, trail paving, free recreation, arts and culture, traffic calming and park improvements. Councillors said traffic calming is the top concern they hear from residents. They also discussed the proposed new staff positions and the enterprise budgets for golf, parking, water and gas.

The meeting was mainly for questions, not final choices. The committee recommended that staff report back before final budget day on a list of follow-up items, including population figures, trail paving, swimming fees, traffic calming and the combined cost of the proposed new positions. Final decisions on the budget come later.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff provide more information on the city's population forecast and confirm the current population against the budget presentation.
The committee recommended that staff explain what the enhanced option for electric vehicle charging stations would achieve, including which vehicles could be electrified.
The committee recommended that staff recirculate a previous trails report and report on whether city staff could do the paving instead of an outside contractor.
The committee recommended that staff provide the youth and adult attendance split and information on non-resident participants for the proposed $2 recreational swim.

The committee recommended that staff report on the cost of different hotspot measures, how many could be installed each year, the point where more staff would be needed, and more mobile radar signs and sponsorship.

decisions.item: Special events and park basketball court
decisions.detail: The committee recommended an issue paper on more events, sponsorship and youth events, and information on the cost of building a neighbourhood basketball court.

decisions.item: Staffing costs and rental water heaters
decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff report the combined cost of all proposed new positions and the costs and rental rates of the water heater rental program {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Several councillors called traffic calming the top issue they hear from residents and supported more money. Staff said the program is really about $250,000 a year, and that permanent hotspot measures work year-round while seasonal flexible signs come down in winter. Some councillors still wanted more flexible signs and radar signs, and one did not support the extra $60,000 for them.

On trail paving, some councillors argued it has been underfunded and links neighbourhoods to schools and supports year-round walking and cycling. Others asked about lighting, which staff said is not in the costing, and about school board cooperation. One councillor wanted the money weighed against other ways to cut greenhouse gases.

On free recreation, councillors supported the $2 swim and expanded leisure access. One suggested holding the swim funding in reserve, or lowering the fee for youth only, and another questioned out-of-town users. Staff said the $2 swim applies to open swims where pool space is not a limit. Staff also said some community centres offer far fewer programs than others, which is why two programming positions are proposed.

On fleet greening, councillors asked for evidence of payback and fuel savings, and one asked whether the money would cut the most greenhouse gases. They also raised the difficulty of getting electric vehicles. Staff said they assume no net cost change for now and will bring back usage and savings data.

On staffing, one councillor questioned the total of about 22 new positions given inflation. Staff said the list was cut from a much longer one and is about 1.5% growth in headcount, below population growth. Councillors also asked about the cost of the contact centre and revenue customer service positions.
